========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, thank you for seeing me, doctor. I just... I came in because I really can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It's gotten so terribly out of hand. 

I mean, if you were to walk into my house right now and look at my kitchen table, you wouldn't even be able to see the wood underneath. It is just completely covered with... well, everything. There are my husband’s appointment papers—he has all these doctors he sees now, and they give you so much paperwork with the instructions and the summaries—and then right mixed in with all of that are the church flyers for our upcoming events, and the notes from the senior center that I brought home weeks ago, and just... oh, I don't even know how many half-finished lists. I write these little lists on scraps of paper thinking they'll help me get my thoughts straight, but they just become part of the mess. 

And the worst part is, I'll sit down at that table in the morning with my tea, and I just look at it all, and I completely freeze. I sit there not knowing which piece of paper I'm supposed to pick up first, or which task to start with, and I just... I get so overwhelmed by the sheer volume of it that I just sit there until the whole day is completely gone. The sun starts going down, and the whole day is wasted, and the pile hasn't moved an inch. It's so embarrassing to live like this at my age, I just don't know how to manage it anymore.

Oh, goodness, yes. It’s... it's not just the table, it’s bleeding into absolutely everything else I’m supposed to be doing. Just the other day, my daughter—she’s so good to us, always checking in—she asked me to run a simple errand for her. I think she needed me to drop something off because she was tied up at work. I promised her I would do it, I really, truly meant to, but... well, the day just slipped right through my fingers and I completely forgot. She had to do it herself after a long shift, and I felt just terrible about it. 

And it's not just her, it's everyone. I’ve missed returning so many phone calls from friends... I'll hear the answering machine click and think, 'I'll call them back right after I make lunch,' and then lunch comes and goes and... I just don't do it. I forget entirely. 

And the mail! Oh, the mail is an absolute nightmare. I’ll bring it inside from the box and set it down on the counter, and before I know it, important bills are just left sitting there, completely buried under a stack of supermarket circulars and junk mail. I don't even realize they're there until we get a late notice in the next batch of mail.

Oh, no, no, it's not like that. I mean, my memory for things that have actually happened is perfectly fine. It's just the... the doing of things that I lose track of. Oh, goodness, anxious... overwhelmed... well, yes and no, I suppose. I mean, it's a very specific sort of feeling. It’s not like the anxiety my sister gets, you know? So, yes, it's overwhelmingly heavy, and it makes me feel just dreadful about myself, but I wouldn't say I get anxious in the sense of... well, in a medical sense, I suppose. I sit there not knowing which piece of paper I'm supposed to pick up first, or which task to start with, and I just... I get so overwhelmed by the sheer volume of it that I just sit there until the whole day is completely gone. The sun starts going down, and the whole day is wasted, and the pile hasn't moved an inch. It's so embarrassing to live like this at my age, I just don't know how to manage it anymore.\n\nDoctor: Are you having trouble completing tasks or responsibilities outside of managing the clutter at home?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, yes. It’s... it's not just the table, it’s bleeding into absolutely everything else I’m supposed to be doing. Just the other day, my daughter—she’s so good to us, always checking in—she asked me to run a simple errand for her. I think she needed me to drop something off because she was tied up at work. I promised her I would do it, I really, truly meant to, but... well, the day just slipped right through my fingers and I completely forgot. She had to do it herself after a long shift, and I felt just terrible about it. \n\nAnd it's not just her, it's everyone. I’ve missed returning so many phone calls from friends... I'll hear the answering machine click and think, 'I'll call them back right after I make lunch,' and then lunch comes and goes and... I just don't do it. I forget entirely. \n\nAnd the mail! Oh, the mail is an absolute nightmare. I’ll bring it inside from the box and set it down on the counter, and before I know it, important bills are just left sitting there, completely buried under a stack of supermarket circulars and junk mail. I don't even realize they're there until we get a late notice in the next batch of mail. \n\nBut I think the most frightening part, the thing that really makes me feel like I'm losing my grip, is my husband’s care. He relies on me so much now, you know? And more than once recently, I’ve realized—entirely too late—that I never actually called to confirm one of his appointments. I’ll be sitting there in the evening watching television and it suddenly hits me like a ton of bricks. I'll think, 'Did I call Dr. Evans' office back?' And of course, I didn't. It’s just... I’m dropping the ball on everything, doctor, not just the house. I just can't seem to hold onto a single thought long enough to see it through.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself forgetting things that happened recently, apart from just forgetting to do tasks?\n\nPatient: Oh, no, no, it's not like that. I mean, my memory for things that have actually happened is perfectly fine. It's just the... the doing of things that I lose track of. Like, I remember perfectly well that my neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives two doors down, lovely woman, always has the most beautiful hydrangeas in the summer—she came over on Tuesday morning. We sat right there in the living room, and she told me all about her grandson's graduation in Ohio, and I remember every detail of that conversation. I remember she wore a yellow sweater, and we had Earl Grey tea, and I remember thinking I should really try to grow hydrangeas again, even though the soil here is so tricky. \n\nSo it's not that my mind is going blank on what's happening around me. If we watch a movie, or if my husband tells me a story about his day, I retain all of that just fine. It's... it's just the tasks. The things I'm supposed to initiate or follow through on. It's like the thoughts of what I need to *do* just evaporate into thin air, but the memories of what I've *experienced* are still right there, clear as a bell. I just... I don't want you to think I'm losing my mind in that way, like dementia or something, because my daughter was worried about that, and I told her, 'Sweetheart, I remember everything you tell me, I just forget to mail the package you asked me to send!' It's a very distinct difference, at least to me. But the forgetting to do things... well, that's bad enough on its own, isn't it?\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you think about all the tasks you're not completing?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, anxious... overwhelmed... well, yes and no, I suppose. I mean, it's a very specific sort of feeling. It’s not like the anxiety my sister gets, you know? She gets these terrible panic attacks where her heart races and she thinks she's having a heart attack—she actually went to the emergency room twice last year for it, and it turned out to just be stress. It’s nothing like that for me. I don't feel my heart pounding or get short of breath or anything physical like that. \n\nBut overwhelmed? Oh, certainly. Like I was saying about sitting at that kitchen table... it's just this heavy, sinking feeling in the pit of my stomach. When I look at all the things I haven't done, it's like... it's like standing at the bottom of a mountain, and you know you have to climb it, but you don't even have your shoes on yet. I just sit there and look at the bills, and the notes, and I think about my husband's appointments, and it just feels like this enormous weight pressing down on me. \n\nAnd then, of course, I feel guilty. The guilt is almost worse than the feeling overwhelmed. I'll lay in bed at night, and instead of just falling asleep like a normal person, my mind will start running through the catalog of everything I dropped the ball on that day. 'I didn't call the pharmacy,' 'I didn't sort the mail,' 'I never finished folding those towels in the laundry basket.' And I just lay there feeling so foolish and useless. I’ve been running a household for nearly fifty years, doctor. Fifty years! I used to host Thanksgiving dinner for twenty-five people, completely by myself, and I had everything timed perfectly right down to the dinner rolls coming out of the oven just as everyone was sitting down. And now... now I can't even manage to sort a stack of envelopes without feeling like I'm drowning. So, yes, it's overwhelmingly heavy, and it makes me feel just dreadful about myself, but I wouldn't say I get anxious in the sense of... well, in a medical sense, I suppose. Just terribly, terribly bogged down by it all.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. Sad? Oh, well... I don't know if I'd use the word depressed. I mean, I certainly don't cry myself to sleep or feel like life isn't worth living, nothing drastic like that. I know some people get so depressed they can't even get out of bed in the morning, and that's not me. I'm up every morning at 6:30, making my husband his oatmeal and getting the coffee started.

And now... now I look at myself and I just feel this profound sense of loss. It makes me sad to think that my daughter has to step in and handle things for me, or that I'm letting my husband down when he needs me most. 

Sometimes I'll be looking through old photo albums—I was doing that just last Sunday, actually, looking at pictures from our 25th anniversary party that I planned entirely by myself—and I'll just feel this lump in my throat. It's just hard, doctor. It's hard to watch yourself slip like this and not be able to stop it, no matter how hard you try. So, yes, I suppose I do feel sad about it, quite sad sometimes, but it's not like a dark cloud hanging over me all day. It's just a quiet sort of heartbreak over losing my... my competence, I guess you could call it.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes, I suppose it is starting to cause some... friction, you might say. It’s hard to admit, really, because I’ve always prided myself on being the one who took care of everyone else. But lately, things have shifted, and not in a way I like. 

Take my daughter, for instance. She’s a wonderful girl, very capable, works as a manager at a bank downtown, so she’s always been very organized. But lately... well, she’s started hovering. That’s the only word for it. She comes over on Sundays for dinner, like she always has, but now, before we even sit down to eat, she’s asking to see the mail pile. She’s double-checking the bills to make sure I’ve paid them, and she’s looking at the calendar on the fridge to make sure I haven’t missed any of my husband’s doctor appointments. And I know she means well, I really do, but it stings. It stings because she’s doing it because she doesn’t trust me to handle it anymore. She knows I’ve let things slip, and now she feels she has to step in and manage me, like I’m a child. It makes me feel so small, doctor. We used to just chat about her week and the grandchildren, and now it feels like an interrogation about my to-do list.

And it’s not just at home, either. It’s affecting my social life, the things I used to love doing. I’ve been involved with the senior center for years—I used to be on the board, actually. Every spring, we put on this big luncheon, a really lovely event with catered food and a silent auction to raise money for local charities. I’ve been the lead organizer for that luncheon for the past six years. I coordinated the caterers, handled the invitations, organized the volunteers... I did it all. But this year... this year I just couldn’t do it. The thought of keeping all those moving parts straight, of remembering to call the florist back, or following up with the auction donors... it just felt impossible. I had to step down. I told them I was just getting too old and wanted to pass the baton, but the truth is, I was terrified I’d ruin the whole event because I couldn’t keep my ducks in a row. 

So, yes, it’s affecting my relationships. I’m pulling back from things I used to lead, and my own daughter is treating me like I need a chaperone for my own life. It’s... it’s just very humbling, and not in a good way.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, exactly. That is exactly it. It’s not that I don’t want to do them—I’m not a lazy person, doctor, I never have been. I wake up every morning with the very best of intentions. I tell myself, "Eleanor, today is the day you clear off that kitchen table." But then I actually sit down and look at what needs to be done, especially if it’s something that takes a lot of real concentration. 

When there’s a form to fill out, or those terrible, dense insurance papers to read for my husband's Medicare supplement... or even something that used to be so simple for me, like trying to put together a program schedule for my garden club... I just... I freeze. I look at the pages, and my head feels completely worn out before I even start. It’s the strangest sensation. It’s not a physical tiredness, it's just... it’s like my brain knows how much work it’s going to take to read the fine print and figure out what goes where, and it just flat out refuses to turn on. 

So, instead of just doing it, I keep finding little reasons to put it off. I’ll be sitting right there with the pen in my hand, staring at the insurance forms, and suddenly I’ll think, "Oh, I really ought to go water the African violets on the windowsill," or "I should probably wipe down the kitchen baseboards before I get deep into this." And I don't even care about the baseboards! I'll end up polishing the good silver that we haven't used since Christmas of 2018, or reorganizing the spice rack—doing absolutely anything just to avoid forcing my mind to focus on those papers. I want to get them done, I truly do, but the thought of the mental effort it takes... it's just so exhausting to even contemplate that I find every excuse under the sun to just walk away from the table. And then the whole day is gone, and the papers are exactly where I left them.

Well, yes, exactly like I was just mentioning with the silver and the spice rack! It’s a terrible cycle, really, and I seem to be doing it all the time now. Like I said, when there’s a form to fill out, or those awful insurance papers to read, or even trying to put together that program schedule for the garden club... Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean... I suppose I like things done nicely, certainly, but I’ve never been a perfectionist. Not really. I’m not one of those women who needs every throw pillow perfectly karate-chopped on the sofa, or who panics if there’s a little typo in a newsletter.

It’s the sheer, exhausting thought of having to corral my brain into focusing on the words on the page. It’s like trying to drive a car with the parking brake engaged. You can press the gas pedal all you want, but you aren't going anywhere, and the engine just whines and strains. That's exactly what my head feels like. 

So I go scrub the bathtub grout instead, not because I'm afraid of doing the paperwork poorly, but because scrubbing grout doesn't require my brain to... to wrestle with itself, if that makes any sense. Motivated? Oh, well... that’s the tricky part, isn't it? Because I *do* want to do them. I really do! It's not a matter of not caring. 

I’ll wake up in the morning, and I’ll say to myself, "Eleanor, today is the day." I’ll even go make a special pot of tea—Earl Grey, usually, with just a little splash of lemon, because I read in one of my magazines that the scent of citrus is supposed to be invigorating for the mind. I’ll lay out my nice pens, I'll turn on the little brass desk lamp, and I'll get everything perfectly ready. So the intention is absolutely there! The desire to just have the wretched things finished and off my mind is there. 

But then... well, it’s exactly what I’ve been saying to you this whole time. The moment I actually sit down and look at the pile... when there’s a form to fill out, or those endless insurance papers to read, or even just that program schedule for the garden club I need to put together... I just keep finding little reasons to put it off. I'll adjust the lamp. I'll notice a smudge on the window glass and think I should just wipe that off really quickly. 

Any motivation I had just completely evaporates, because my head feels so terribly worn out before I even start. It’s not that I don't want to be motivated, doctor, it's just that my motivation can't seem to survive that heavy, exhausted feeling that washes over my brain the second I realize I have to actually do the work. It’s like my battery goes from fully charged to completely dead just by looking at the paperwork! So despite all my good intentions and my Earl Grey tea, I just can't push through that mental wall, and I end up back in the bathroom scrubbing grout again.

Less interest? Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that. If anything, I think I enjoy my little hobbies just as much as I ever did, perhaps even more now that I have the time to really savor them. 

Take my flower arranging, for instance. My knees aren't quite what they used to be for getting down in the dirt and doing the actual planting, though I do still try to keep the front window boxes looking cheerful, but the arranging part... oh, I still absolutely adore it. I was completely absorbed in it! I didn't feel heavy or exhausted or drained in the slightest while I was doing that. It was just a pure joy. 

And I still love reading my historical novels, too, and trying out new baking recipes when the mood strikes. I just finished a fascinating book about the Tudor dynasty last week. So, no, I haven't lost my spark for the things I love. The interest is very much still there. 

The problem, really, is just that I end up doing those fun things—like fussing with Mildred's hydrangeas or reading about King Henry—when I *should* be doing the Medicare forms or paying the electric bill! I'll happily spend an entire afternoon doing something I enjoy just to avoid looking at a pile of paperwork. So, no, doctor, no loss of interest at all. I still love my life and my little projects, it's truly just the dreadful, tedious tasks that I can't seem to make my brain cooperate with.

But this year... this year I just couldn’t do it. The thought of keeping all those moving parts straight, of remembering to call the florist back, or following up with the auction donors... it just felt impossible. I had to step down. I told them I was just getting too old and wanted to pass the baton, but the truth is, I was terrified I’d ruin the whole event because I couldn’t keep my ducks in a row. \n\nSo, yes, it’s affecting my relationships. I’m pulling back from things I used to lead, and my own daughter is treating me like I need a chaperone for my own life. It’s... it’s just very humbling, and not in a good way.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you want to do these tasks, but just can't seem to get started or follow through?\n\nPatient: Oh, exactly. That is exactly it. It’s not that I don’t want to do them—I’m not a lazy person, doctor, I never have been. I wake up every morning with the very best of intentions. I tell myself, \"Eleanor, today is the day you clear off that kitchen table.\" But then I actually sit down and look at what needs to be done, especially if it’s something that takes a lot of real concentration. \n\nWhen there’s a form to fill out, or those terrible, dense insurance papers to read for my husband's Medicare supplement... or even something that used to be so simple for me, like trying to put together a program schedule for my garden club... I just... I freeze. I look at the pages, and my head feels completely worn out before I even start. It’s the strangest sensation. It’s not a physical tiredness, it's just... it’s like my brain knows how much work it’s going to take to read the fine print and figure out what goes where, and it just flat out refuses to turn on. \n\nSo, instead of just doing it, I keep finding little reasons to put it off. I’ll be sitting right there with the pen in my hand, staring at the insurance forms, and suddenly I’ll think, \"Oh, I really ought to go water the African violets on the windowsill,\" or \"I should probably wipe down the kitchen baseboards before I get deep into this.\" And I don't even care about the baseboards! I'll end up polishing the good silver that we haven't used since Christmas of 2018, or reorganizing the spice rack—doing absolutely anything just to avoid forcing my mind to focus on those papers. I want to get them done, I truly do, but the thought of the mental effort it takes... it's just so exhausting to even contemplate that I find every excuse under the sun to just walk away from the table. And then the whole day is gone, and the papers are exactly where I left them.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself doing other activities to avoid tasks that you feel are overwhelming or too difficult?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, exactly like I was just mentioning with the silver and the spice rack! It’s a terrible cycle, really, and I seem to be doing it all the time now. Like I said, when there’s a form to fill out, or those awful insurance papers to read, or even trying to put together that program schedule for the garden club... I just keep finding little reasons to put it off. And it really is because my head feels completely worn out before I even start. \n\nIt’s like my brain is desperately looking for an escape hatch. Now, nobody has used that bathtub since my grandson stayed over during Thanksgiving of 2021, but suddenly, cleaning that grout was the most urgent thing in the world. I spent nearly two hours on my hands and knees scrubbing just so I wouldn't have to look at those insurance papers. \n\nAnd the whole time, I knew I should be at the kitchen table. I kept telling myself, 'Eleanor, you need to go read those forms,' but the thought of trying to make sense of the deductibles and the copays... it just felt like trying to climb a mountain. My mind was exhausted just anticipating the effort it would take to concentrate. So I just kept scrubbing. I’ll reorganize the linen closet by color, I’ll iron my husband's undershirts, I'll deadhead all the geraniums on the back patio... absolutely anything to avoid the tasks that make my brain feel that heavy, tired feeling. It's so frustrating because I know exactly what I'm doing while I'm doing it, but I just can't seem to stop myself from finding a distraction to avoid the real work.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you avoid these tasks because you're afraid of not doing them perfectly or making mistakes?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean... I suppose I like things done nicely, certainly, but I’ve never been a perfectionist. Not really. I’m not one of those women who needs every throw pillow perfectly karate-chopped on the sofa, or who panics if there’s a little typo in a newsletter. \n\nHeavens, back when I was running the senior center luncheons I told you about, things went wrong all the time! I remember one year the caterer brought chicken instead of the baked salmon we ordered, and we just rolled with it. I didn't fall to pieces over a mistake. It’s like trying to drive a car with the parking brake engaged. You can press the gas pedal all you want, but you aren't going anywhere, and the engine just whines and strains. Heavens, I've lived seventy years, I've failed at plenty of things in my time and survived just fine! I remember back in, oh, it must have been 1984, I tried to make a baked Alaska for a dinner party with my husband's boss, and the entire thing just melted into a soupy puddle right there on the good dining room table. Overwhelmed? Well... I suppose you could use that word, doctor, but it’s not quite a panicked sort of overwhelmed, if you see what I mean. I don't feel like I'm drowning in anxiety or anything like that. It’s really exactly what I was just trying to explain a moment ago about sitting at my desk.

Pleasure? Oh, I don't know if pleasure is the right word at all, doctor. Relief, certainly. A great, big, heavy sigh of relief that the dreadful thing is finally out of my house and out of my mind! But pleasure? No, I wouldn't say that. 

It's not like the feeling I get when I step back and look at a perfectly balanced vase of those blue hydrangeas, where you feel that little warm glow in your chest and you think, 'Oh, didn't that turn out beautifully?' That's pleasure. That's joy. 

When I finally finish the paperwork... well, take last month, for example. I finally, *finally* managed to finish a renewal form for my supplemental health insurance. I had put it off for weeks, moving it from the kitchen counter to the dining table, then to the little desk in the hallway, just shuffling it around like a bad penny. When I finally forced myself to sit down, read the tiny print, fill in all the little boxes, and actually put the stamp on the envelope... I didn't feel a sense of accomplishment or happiness. I didn't want to celebrate. I just felt completely wrung out. 

My sister, Eleanor—she lives over in Scottsdale now, we talk every Sunday—she's one of those people who gets a genuine thrill out of crossing things off a to-do list. She actually color-codes her lists with those little gel pens! She tells me, 'Oh, it feels so wonderful to get things done, it gives me such a boost.' But for me, it just feels like... well, like I've just survived a terrible ordeal. I just want to go lie down on the sofa with a cup of Earl Grey tea and a biscuit and close my eyes for an hour. 

So no, I wouldn't call it pleasure. Just a very tired, desperate sort of relief that the dark cloud has passed and I don't have to look at the wretched papers anymore.

That's exactly what my head feels like. \n\nSo I go scrub the bathtub grout instead, not because I'm afraid of doing the paperwork poorly, but because scrubbing grout doesn't require my brain to... to wrestle with itself, if that makes any sense. I don't need to be perfect. I just want it done, doctor. Perfect or not, I just simply cannot seem to make myself do the actual *doing* of it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you avoid these tasks because you're afraid of failing at them?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying about making mistakes, doctor, no, not at all. It really feels like the same sort of thing, doesn't it? I’m truly not afraid of failing. I mean... what is there to actually fail at when you’re just reading a Medicare supplement or writing down a list of dates for the garden club? \n\nIf I do a terrible job on the schedule, what’s the worst that happens? Mildred from down the street complains that the font is too small, or we accidentally double-book a guest speaker on the day we're supposed to be doing our spring floral arrangements. It's just not the end of the world. I don't sit at the kitchen table trembling that I'm going to ruin everything or that people are going to judge me. Heavens, I've lived seventy years, I've failed at plenty of things in my time and survived just fine! I remember back in, oh, it must have been 1984, I tried to make a baked Alaska for a dinner party with my husband's boss, and the entire thing just melted into a soupy puddle right there on the good dining room table. We just laughed and served them store-bought cookies. So, no, failure doesn't frighten me in the slightest. \n\nIt really, truly just comes back to that... that heavy, impossible feeling I was trying to describe. It’s like... well, I don't know if you’ve ever had to push a stalled car? My husband and I had this awful, heavy station wagon back in the seventies, one of those big Ford Country Squires with the fake wood paneling on the side, and one time it broke down right in the middle of a busy intersection. Trying to physically push that massive, heavy car out of the way... that is exactly what it feels like trying to push my brain to start these tasks. \n\nIt's not that I'm afraid the car is going to crash, or that I'm going to push it wrong, or fail at pushing it. It's just that I stand there looking at this huge, heavy thing, and I feel completely drained before I even put my hands on the bumper. My brain just says, 'No, Eleanor, we simply do not have the energy to push this today.' And so I walk away. I go scrub the bathtub, or I polish the silver, because those things don't feel like pushing a station wagon. So, no, it's never about being afraid I'll fail. It's just that I can't seem to find the mental strength to even get the wheels turning.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel motivated to do these tasks when you're not avoiding them?\n\nPatient: Motivated? Oh, well... that’s the tricky part, isn't it? Because I *do* want to do them. I really do! It's not a matter of not caring. \n\nI’ll wake up in the morning, and I’ll say to myself, \"Eleanor, today is the day.\" I’ll even go make a special pot of tea—Earl Grey, usually, with just a little splash of lemon, because I read in one of my magazines that the scent of citrus is supposed to be invigorating for the mind. I’ll go sit down at the lovely oak roll-top desk my husband bought me for our anniversary back in... oh, 1998, I think it was. I’ll lay out my nice pens, I'll turn on the little brass desk lamp, and I'll get everything perfectly ready. So the intention is absolutely there! The desire to just have the wretched things finished and off my mind is there. \n\nBut then... well, it’s exactly what I’ve been saying to you this whole time. I just keep finding little reasons to put it off. I'll adjust the lamp. I'll notice a smudge on the window glass and think I should just wipe that off really quickly. \n\nAny motivation I had just completely evaporates, because my head feels so terribly worn out before I even start. It’s not that I don't want to be motivated, doctor, it's just that my motivation can't seem to survive that heavy, exhausted feeling that washes over my brain the second I realize I have to actually do the work. It’s like my battery goes from fully charged to completely dead just by looking at the paperwork! So despite all my good intentions and my Earl Grey tea, I just can't push through that mental wall, and I end up back in the bathroom scrubbing grout again.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself having less interest in doing things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Less interest? Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that. If anything, I think I enjoy my little hobbies just as much as I ever did, perhaps even more now that I have the time to really savor them. \n\nTake my flower arranging, for instance. My knees aren't quite what they used to be for getting down in the dirt and doing the actual planting, though I do still try to keep the front window boxes looking cheerful, but the arranging part... oh, I still absolutely adore it. Well, motivation... you know, people talk about motivation like it's this magical switch you can just flip on, like turning on a lamp in a dark room. And I suppose if I had it, really had it, maybe things would be different? But doctor, I know I keep saying this, and you must be getting terribly sick of hearing it, but I just can't seem to make it clear enough. It's not just a matter of wanting to do it or not wanting to do it. 

Take that garden club program schedule I've been mentioning. I actually *want* to do it. I've been a member for fifteen years, I love the ladies in the club, and Mrs. Higgins is really depending on me to get the dates right for the spring luncheon and the guest speakers. I really do want to be helpful and get it printed on that nice heavy cardstock we use. That's motivation, isn't it? I have the motivation! 

But the moment I actually sit down at the desk and think about organizing it all... or when I have to look at those dreadful insurance papers again, or any sort of official form with the tiny little boxes... I just start finding all these little reasons to put it off. I'll think, "Oh, I need to find a better pen," or "I should really wipe down the baseboards in the hallway first, they're looking terribly dusty," or "Let me just check the mail one more time." 

And I do all that because... well, like I've been trying to say, my head just feels completely, entirely worn out before I even make the first mark on the paper. It's like a car running out of gas before you even back out of the driveway. So even if I felt incredibly motivated—even if someone offered me a trip to Paris to just sit and fill out a form—I think my brain would still hit that wall. The mental fatigue is just right there, waiting for me, before I've even begun. 

Does that make sense? Because I feel like we keep circling back to this, and I just want you to understand how physically tiring the very thought of the work is for me, regardless of how much I might want to get it done. It's a dreadful feeling, really it is.

Doctor, I... well, I feel like we are going in circles just a bit here, aren't we? I know you're trying to get to the bottom of this, and I appreciate your thoroughness, I really do, but as I was just saying a moment ago about motivation... it really isn't about that. I feel like I'm beating a dead horse, and I apologize if I'm coming across as difficult, but I just don't know how else to explain it so you understand the physical reality of it. 

It truly doesn't matter if I have all the motivation in the world, or if I wake up feeling particularly sprightly and determined to conquer the day. The simple truth is, whenever there is one of those long forms to fill out, or those terribly complicated insurance papers I have to read through, or even that program schedule for the garden club... I will inevitably keep finding little reasons to put it off. I’ll go reorganize the spice rack, or I'll scrub a perfectly clean sink, or I'll just stand there staring out the window at the neighbor's cat for twenty minutes. 

And I do all of that because my head just feels completely, utterly worn out before I even start. It's not a lack of drive or desire. It's that the mental effort required just drains me before I've even picked up the pen. My late husband, Arthur, he used to handle all the paperwork. He'd sit at his heavy oak desk—the one we bought at an antique show in 1982, a beautiful piece of furniture, really—and he'd just breeze right through it all with his reading glasses perched on his nose. But me? Just looking at a stack of papers makes my brain feel like it's suddenly full of lead. 

So, no, feeling more motivated wouldn't fix it, because the exhaustion is already there, blocking the path. Do you see what I mean? I just don't know how to get past that heavy, worn-out feeling in my head, no matter how much I might want to.
